channel.title: Five Wisdom Traditions
channel.description: Five-minute conversations on the common principles of the major religions and the most-quoted passages of the Bible, the Tao Te Ching, the Quran, the Buddhist sutras and Confucius: what they meant, how they are used today, and how to live them. Voices are AI-generated with the open-source Kokoro text-to-speech model.
channel.itunes:author: Five Wisdom Traditions
channel.itunes:summary: Five-minute conversations on the common principles of the major religions and the most-quoted passages of five wisdom traditions.

item.title: Welcome
item.description: An introduction to the Primer: where it comes from, its three ground rules, its goal, the eight sages it draws on, and how its chapters are organized.
item.content:encoded:
An introduction to the Primer: where it comes from, its three ground rules, its goal, the eight sages it draws on, and how its chapters are organized.

This is Five Wisdom Traditions. Today we open the Primer, a short guide to the principles the world's great teachers hold in common.

So before we start, where does this Primer come from?

It's adapted from a discussion series called Common Principles of the Major Religions. And it starts from a simple observation. Many of the world's great teachers lived thousands of miles and hundreds of years apart, yet they kept arriving at the same truths about how to live.

That's a big claim. How does the Primer show it?

By putting their words side by side, one life question at a time, and letting them speak for themselves. You hear Jesus, then Lao Tzu, then the Buddha, then Confucius, all on the same question.

I like that. It feels less like an argument and more like a conversation around a table.

That's exactly the spirit. The original series ran with three ground rules, and they work just as well if you're reading alone. The first is short. Open mind.

Easy to say, harder to do.

Sure. The second is, learn from countless sages. And the third is, maintain respect for all religions, philosophies and virtuous ones.

Virtuous ones. So the respect goes to good people too, wherever they come from.

Right. Those three rules set the tone. Nobody is asked to give up their own tradition. You're asked to listen generously to the others.

And what's the point of all this listening? What's the series actually after?

It states its goal in one line. To awaken: go beyond the mundane world to something bigger than ourselves.

Go beyond the mundane world. That sounds lofty, but I think most of us know the feeling. You're stuck in errands and worries, and then something reminds you there's more to life than the to-do list.

That's a good way to put it. The Primer treats awakening as something you can work toward, step by step, through very ordinary virtues.

Who are the teachers we'll be hearing from?

The Primer names eight sages. The earliest is Abraham, about four thousand years ago, honored by Jews, Christians and Muslims alike. Then Lao Tzu, the teacher of the Tao, about twenty-six centuries ago. Around the same time came Sakyamuni Buddha, the founder of Buddhism.

And Confucius is in there, I assume.

He is, about twenty-five centuries ago. And his great follower Mencius, a couple of centuries after him. Then Jesus, about two thousand years ago. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, born around the year five seventy. And finally Hui-neng, a Chinese Zen master born around the year six thirty-eight.

That's quite a spread. Four thousand years, and from the Middle East to China.

And that spread is what makes the agreement so striking. They didn't read each other. They couldn't have.

So how is the Primer laid out? If I open it, what do I find?

Each chapter takes one principle. It explains the principle briefly, gives the sages' words in parallel, offers a few questions to discuss or journal about, and links to related passages elsewhere in the app.

And what's the order of the chapters?

It begins with what the series calls its backbone, the Five Constant Virtues. Then a chapter on purpose in life. Then one chapter each on benevolence, propriety, righteousness, wisdom, and faith and sincerity.

The virtues one by one.

Exactly. After that come the practices that put the virtues to work. Peacemaking and forgiveness. Introspection, repentance and vows. Cause and effect, and how to transform your destiny. The path of cultivation. The six paramitas from Buddhism. The five human relationships, where virtue is actually lived. And it closes with a chapter on awakening.

Do I have to read it in order?

Not at all. The Primer says you can read it straight through, jump to any chapter, or skip it entirely. The quotes are always one tap away.

That takes the pressure off.

Here's a practice for today. Take five quiet minutes and read the three ground rules again: open mind, learn from countless sages, respect all religions, philosophies and virtuous ones. Then notice one moment today where you'd normally dismiss a view you disagree with, and listen a little longer instead.

And a question to sit with?

It's the one the series itself keeps returning to. Why are you born into this world, and for what purpose?

We'll be coming back to that one.

Thanks for listening to Five Wisdom Traditions.

item.title: The Five Constant Virtues
item.description: The backbone of the Primer: benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom and faith, their links to the five elements and the five Buddhist precepts, and Mencius's four beginnings.
item.content:encoded:
The backbone of the Primer: benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom and faith, their links to the five elements and the five Buddhist precepts, and Mencius's four beginnings.

This is Five Wisdom Traditions. Today we look at the Five Constant Virtues, the backbone of the whole Primer.

Five virtues. Which five?

Benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom, and faith, which the Primer also calls sincerity. The series says these five appear, under different names, in every tradition.

They sound very Confucian.

The names come from Chinese thought, yes. But what's interesting is that the same ethic shows up in three vocabularies. Chinese philosophy links each virtue to one of the five elements. And Buddhism links each one to one of the five precepts.

Okay, walk me through that. Start with benevolence.

Benevolence is linked to wood, and to the precept of no killing.

Wood makes sense. Something growing, alive. And not taking life is the most basic form of caring for it.

Nicely put. Next is righteousness. Its element is metal, and its precept is no stealing.

Metal. Firm, a little hard. Righteousness has that edge to it. You don't bend on what belongs to someone else.

Third is propriety, linked to fire, and to the precept of no sexual misconduct.

Fire is warm and it's also dangerous. I guess propriety is about keeping that warmth in its right place.

That's a fair reading. Fourth, wisdom, linked to water, and to the precept of no intoxicants.

Oh, that one's clever. Water is clear. Intoxicants cloud the mind.

And water comes back again and again in these traditions as the model of wisdom. Last is faith, or sincerity. Its element is earth, and its precept is no lying.

Earth, the ground under everything. If you can't trust someone's word, nothing else holds up.

So you see the pattern. Five virtues, five elements, five precepts. Three different cultures describing the same shape of a good life.

Here's my newcomer question. Are these rules we're supposed to obey? Because rules imposed from outside rarely stick with me.

That's exactly where Mencius comes in. He taught that these virtues are not imposed from outside at all. Everyone is born with their seeds. He called them the four beginnings.

Four, not five?

Four. Mencius names the first four virtues, each with a feeling at its root. Here are his words. The feeling of commiseration is the principle of benevolence. The feeling of shame and dislike is the principle of righteousness.

So benevolence starts as a feeling, that pang when someone else is hurting.

Right. He continues. The feeling of modesty and complaisance is the principle of propriety. The feeling of approving and disapproving is the principle of knowledge.

Knowledge there meaning wisdom.

Yes. And then the line that makes it memorable. Men have these four principles just as they have their four limbs.

That's a great image. Nobody had to teach me to have arms.

Exactly. You still have to train them, though. A child is born with legs but has to learn to walk. Mencius thought virtue works the same way. The seed is already there. Our job is to grow it.

That changes how I'd think about being a good person. It's less about acquiring something foreign and more about not crushing something that's already trying to grow.

And that's why the Primer calls these the constant virtues. They don't change with fashion or culture. Each of the next five chapters takes one of them in turn.

How would someone actually use this in daily life?

One way is to treat the five as a kind of mirror. At the end of the day you ask, was I kind today? Was I fair? Was I respectful? Did I see clearly? Was I honest?

Five questions. That's manageable.

So here's a practice for today. Watch for one of the four beginnings showing up in you. A moment of sympathy, a flash of shame at something wrong, a small courtesy you offer without thinking, or a clear sense that something is right or wrong. When you notice it, pause and name it. That's the seed.

And the reflection question?

It comes straight from the chapter. Which of the five virtues comes most naturally to you? Which is hardest?

I already know my answer to the second half.

Thanks for listening to Five Wisdom Traditions.

item.title: Purpose in Life
item.description: Why are we here? Jesus, Lao Tzu, the Prophet Muhammad, Hui-neng and Confucius on letting go of the small self, storing up lasting treasure, and staying soft and yielding.
item.content:encoded:
Why are we here? Jesus, Lao Tzu, the Prophet Muhammad, Hui-neng and Confucius on letting go of the small self, storing up lasting treasure, and staying soft and yielding.

This is Five Wisdom Traditions. Today's question is the biggest one of all: what is our purpose in life?

No small topic. Where does the Primer even begin?

It notices that every tradition answers in a similar way. Let go of the small self. Store up treasure that can't be stolen. And stay soft and yielding.

Three ideas. Let's take them one at a time.

Start with letting go of the self. Jesus says, in Matthew chapter sixteen, For whoever wants to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for My sake will find it.

That's a paradox. Lose your life to find it.

Christians read it as giving yourself over to God and to others. And many people from every background recognize the experience. The times we feel most alive are usually the times we forget about ourselves for a while.

Like caring for someone who's sick, or getting lost in good work.

Exactly. The second idea is treasure. In Matthew chapter six, Jesus says, Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy. And then, But store up for yourselves treasures in heaven.

Moth and rust. That's very concrete. Everything I own is slowly falling apart.

And the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, made a similar point in a saying recorded by al-Bukhari. Be in the world as if you were a stranger or a traveller along the path.

A traveller. I like that. You can enjoy the inn, but you don't move in.

That's the spirit. A traveller packs light and keeps their eyes on where they're going. The Quran gives that direction. And whoever holds firmly to Allah has indeed been guided to a straight path.

So purpose has to do with direction, more than possessions.

Yes. Now the third idea, softness. Lao Tzu, in chapter seventy-six of the Tao Te Ching, says, Whoever is stiff and inflexible is a disciple of death. Whoever is soft and yielding is a disciple of life.

That's counterintuitive. We usually admire the strong, unbending person.

He goes on. The hard and stiff will be broken. The soft and supple will prevail. And in chapter seventy-eight, he gives his favorite image. There is nothing in the world more soft and weak than water, and yet for attacking things that are firm and strong there is nothing that can take precedence of it.

Water wearing down stone.

The series puts it beautifully. The aim is to overcome all the challenges thrown at us in life with a sort of softness, to let love guide us, to learn with a flexibility, patience, kindness as we grow.

Where does Buddhism fit into this?

The Primer quotes Hui-neng, the Zen master. His famous verse is, There is no bodhi tree, nor stand of a mirror bright. Since all is void, where can the dust alight?

That one I'll need help with.

Another monk had written that the mind is like a mirror you must keep polishing. Hui-neng answered that the deepest self was never dusty to begin with. Purpose, for him, is seeing through the small self we keep polishing and protecting.

So that's the letting go again, from another angle.

And Confucius widens it out to the whole society. In the Book of Rites he describes the great harmony. When the great principle prevails, the world is a commonwealth. Men do not regard as parents only their own parents, nor treat as children only their own children.

So purpose isn't only personal. It's about how wide your circle of care becomes.

That's how the Primer reads it. Lose the small self, and the family gets bigger.

How would I live this on an ordinary Tuesday?

Here's a practice. Today, notice one moment where you want to dig in and be rigid. An argument, a plan that goes wrong, a delay. Try being like water for a minute. Yield a little, and see what flows around the obstacle.

And the question to carry with us?

It's from the chapter itself. What treasure are you storing up that no thief can steal?

That one's going to follow me around today.

Thanks for listening to Five Wisdom Traditions.

item.title: Benevolence
item.description: The first and root virtue: Mencius's child at the well, the Good Samaritan, the ants in a forest fire, and the Golden Rule across traditions.
item.content:encoded:
The first and root virtue: Mencius's child at the well, the Good Samaritan, the ants in a forest fire, and the Golden Rule across traditions.

This is Five Wisdom Traditions. Today we explore benevolence, the first and root of the five virtues.

Benevolence. It's a slightly old-fashioned word. What does the Primer mean by it?

A natural, inborn compassion. The Primer's subtitle calls it the mind that cannot bear others' suffering.

Inborn. So we're back to Mencius and his seeds.

We are. He gives one of the most famous examples in Chinese philosophy. Imagine anyone who suddenly sees a child about to fall into a well. They feel alarm and distress.

Of course. Anyone would.

That's his point. Mencius says they don't feel it to win the parents' favor, or the neighbors' praise. The heart simply cannot bear it. In his words, The feeling of commiseration is the principle of benevolence.

So the proof that benevolence is natural is that split second before you think.

Exactly. Before any calculation. The series actually teaches benevolence through three stories. That's the first one, the child at the well.

What are the other two?

The second is the Good Samaritan, from the teaching of Jesus. A man is beaten by robbers on the road to Jericho and left half dead. Religious people pass by on the other side. Then a Samaritan, someone from a group the listeners looked down on, stops, bandages him, and pays for his care.

So the hero is the outsider.

Yes. The story comes in answer to a question about the commandment, Love your neighbor as yourself. That's from Mark chapter twelve. The Samaritan shows that your neighbor is whoever is in need in front of you.

And the third story?

The ants in a forest fire. When fire sweeps toward an ant colony, the ants roll into a ball around their queen. The ball rolls through the flames. The ants on the outside give their lives so that the colony survives.

That's moving. Even an ant has that instinct to protect.

And Buddhism expresses the same care in the Metta Sutta, the discourse on loving-kindness. Even as a mother protects with her life her child, her only child, so with a boundless heart should one cherish all living beings.

A boundless heart. So the mother's love is the model, but it has to stretch to everyone.

Right. Now Confucius adds something practical. He asks where benevolence is first learned. His student Youzi says, Filial piety and fraternal submission! Are they not the root of all benevolent actions?

So it starts at home. With your parents and your brothers and sisters.

That's the Confucian view. You practice care in the family, and then it grows outward. And when his student Zigong asked for one word to guide a whole life, Confucius answered, Is not reciprocity such a word? What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others.

The Golden Rule, basically.

The same rule Jesus gives, put the other way around. And there's one more line from Confucius in this chapter. The wise are free from perplexities; the virtuous from anxiety; and the bold from fear.

The virtuous are free from anxiety. Why would kindness make you less anxious?

Think about it. When your mind is on helping someone, there's less room left to worry about yourself. A benevolent heart is a quieter heart.

That's true in my experience. The worst days are the ones spent inside my own head.

So here's a practice for today. Look for one small chance to be a Samaritan. Someone struggling with bags, a coworker who seems overwhelmed, a stranger who's lost. Act before you talk yourself out of it, the way you would for a child near a well.

And the question to reflect on?

Straight from the chapter. Who is the man on the road to Jericho in your life this week?

I have a feeling I already know. And it's probably someone I've been walking past.

That's often how it goes. The Samaritan was simply on the road, and he stopped.

Thanks for listening to Five Wisdom Traditions.

item.title: Propriety
item.description: Love shown in the right manner: Confucius on the rules of propriety, Mencius on respect, Paul on humility, and Lao Tzu's warning about empty form.
item.content:encoded:
Love shown in the right manner: Confucius on the rules of propriety, Mencius on respect, Paul on humility, and Lao Tzu's warning about empty form.

This is Five Wisdom Traditions. Today's virtue is propriety, which the Primer describes as love shown in the right manner.

Propriety sounds like etiquette. Which fork to use.

It includes that, but it goes much deeper. The Chinese word is li. The Primer explains that its character combines divine and offering. Originally it meant a rite, an offering made with reverence.

So it started as something sacred.

Yes. And the Primer says it's a rite that trains us to transform our disposition for the better. Outward respect flowing from inner benevolence.

So benevolence is the feeling, and propriety is the form it takes.

Exactly. The series says love needs connection, so we show love in the right manner. You can love your grandmother deeply, but if you never call, never visit, never say thank you, how does she know?

Fair point. Love that never shows up isn't much use to anyone.

Confucius took this very seriously. In the Analects, book twenty, he says, Without an acquaintance with the rules of propriety, it is impossible for the character to be established.

Strong words. Character depends on manners?

On practiced respect, let's say. When his student Yan Yuan asked about perfect virtue, Confucius said, To subdue one's self and return to propriety is perfect virtue. And then he gave four short rules. Look not at what is contrary to propriety; listen not to what is contrary to propriety; speak not what is contrary to propriety; make no movement which is contrary to propriety.

Look, listen, speak, move. That covers pretty much everything.

It does. It's a discipline of the senses. What you let in and what you put out.

I can see how that would apply now. What we scroll past, what we repeat, how we talk to people online.

Very much so. Mencius then shows why it matters. The benevolent man loves others. The man of propriety shows respect to others. He who loves others is constantly loved by them. He who respects others is constantly respected by them.

So respect comes back to you.

It tends to. And the Apostle Paul, writing to the Philippians, says something very close. Do nothing out of selfish ambition or vain conceit. Rather, in humility value others above yourselves.

Value others above yourselves. That's propriety from the inside.

Right. Now, the Primer is careful to give a counterweight, and it comes from Lao Tzu. He warns that rules without the Tao become just an outer show.

Ah. So you can be perfectly polite and completely cold.

Exactly. The Primer puts it neatly. Form without heart is empty, and heart without form often goes astray.

I like that balance. Most of us lean one way or the other. Either stiff and correct, or warm and a bit careless.

And there's a lovely line the Primer borrows from the writer Madeleine L'Engle, in A Wrinkle in Time. Life is like a sonnet: you're given the form, but you have to write the sonnet yourself.

So the rituals and courtesies are the fourteen lines. What you put in them is yours.

That's it. The form gives shape to the feeling. Then the feeling gives life to the form.

Is there a place where Christianity talks about love's manners like this?

Paul's famous passage in First Corinthians, chapter thirteen, comes close. Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up, doth not behave itself unseemly.

Doth not behave itself unseemly. That's propriety in King James English.

So here's a practice for today. Pick one small courtesy and do it with full attention. Say thank you while looking the person in the eye. Hold a door and mean it. Let the form carry real warmth.

And the reflection question?

From the chapter. What small courtesy, such as please and thank you, has the biggest effect on your relationships?

For me it might just be listening without checking my phone.

Thanks for listening to Five Wisdom Traditions.

item.title: Righteousness
item.description: The moral disposition to do good: Confucius on righteousness and gain, the Quran on what true righteousness is, James on faith and works, and how love makes us fearless.
item.content:encoded:
The moral disposition to do good: Confucius on righteousness and gain, the Quran on what true righteousness is, James on faith and works, and how love makes us fearless.

This is Five Wisdom Traditions. Today's virtue is righteousness, which the series defines as the moral disposition to do good.

Righteousness is a word that makes some people nervous. It can sound like self-righteousness.

That's a real danger, and the traditions know it. But the Primer's definition is practical. It gives righteousness two parts. The first is the willingness to act.

Okay. Knowing what's right isn't enough. You have to actually do it.

And the second part is the ability to manage fear and anxiety so you can keep acting.

That's interesting. I wouldn't have put fear into a definition of righteousness.

But think about when you've failed to do the right thing. Was it because you didn't know? Or because you were afraid?

Honestly, usually afraid. Of looking foolish, of conflict, of losing something.

That's why the series' key insight is so short. With love one is fearless.

So benevolence feeds righteousness. If you care enough, the fear shrinks.

Exactly. Now, Confucius frames righteousness by contrast. In the Analects, book four, he says, The mind of the superior man is conversant with righteousness; the mind of the mean man is conversant with gain.

Mean there means petty, I assume. Small-minded.

Right. It's about what your mind naturally turns to. And in book sixteen he describes the good person this way. When he sees gain to be got, he thinks of righteousness.

That's a useful habit. The moment you see an advantage, you stop and ask if it's fair.

A simple test for business, for politics, for splitting the bill at dinner.

What does the Quran say?

Surah Al-Baqarah, chapter two, verse one seventy-seven, is one of the clearest statements anywhere. Righteousness is not that you turn your faces toward the east or the west.

Meaning which direction you pray?

Yes. The verse says outward ritual alone isn't the heart of it. It continues. But righteous is the one who believes in God, the Last Day, the angels, the Book and the prophets; who gives wealth, despite loving it, to relatives, orphans, the needy, the traveler.

Despite loving it. That's an honest detail. Giving is hard because we like our money.

The Quran admits that. The verse goes on to keeping promises and being patient in hardship. Belief and action belong together.

That sounds like the Letter of James.

It does. James writes, You see that a person is justified by works and not by faith alone. And the prophet Micah, in the Hebrew Bible, sums it up in one line. What doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?

Do justly, love mercy, walk humbly. I could put that on my fridge.

Many people do. Notice it pairs justice with mercy and humility. That's the cure for self-righteousness.

Good. Because that's what worries me. People who are very sure they're right can be awful.

The Primer ends this chapter with a quote from Martin Luther that answers that worry. This life therefore is not righteousness, but growth in righteousness, not being but becoming.

Becoming. So nobody gets to declare themselves finished.

Right. Righteousness is a direction you're walking in, and you're always still on the road.

How do I know what's right in the moment, though? Life is messy.

The chapter asks that too. Part of the answer is in those quotes. Ask whether you're thinking of gain or of what's right. Ask whether your faith is showing up in your actions. And ask whether you're acting with mercy and humility.

And then, if it's right, do it even though you're nervous.

That's the second half of the definition. So here's a practice for today. Notice one small moment where you see the right thing to do and feel a flicker of fear. Speaking up in a meeting, returning extra change, admitting a mistake. Let love for the people involved carry you through, and act.

And the reflection question?

From the chapter. What fear most often stops you from doing the right thing?

That's going to take more than five minutes to answer.

Thanks for listening to Five Wisdom Traditions.

item.title: Wisdom
item.description: Knowing yourself: Lao Tzu, Confucius, Hui-neng and Proverbs on where wisdom comes from, why it is already within us, and why its model is water.
item.content:encoded:
Knowing yourself: Lao Tzu, Confucius, Hui-neng and Proverbs on where wisdom comes from, why it is already within us, and why its model is water.

This is Five Wisdom Traditions. Today's virtue is wisdom, and the Primer begins with a simple claim: wisdom begins with knowing yourself.

That's an old idea. Know thyself.

It shows up everywhere. The Primer says wisdom is already inside everyone, uncovered by reflection and by accepting correction. And its model is water.

Let's start with knowing yourself.

Lao Tzu puts it memorably in chapter thirty-three of the Tao Te Ching. Knowing others is intelligence; knowing yourself is true wisdom. Mastering others is strength; mastering yourself is true power.

I like that it's a pair. You can be very clever about other people and still a mystery to yourself.

Exactly. Plenty of people can read a room. Fewer can read their own motives.

How do you get to know yourself, practically?

The traditions suggest a few ways. One is honesty about what you don't know. Confucius once said to his student Yu, When you know a thing, to hold that you know it; and when you do not know a thing, to allow that you do not know it, this is knowledge.

That's harder than it sounds. Saying I don't know feels risky.

And yet it's where learning starts. Confucius was humble about himself, too. In the Analects, book seven, he says, I am not one who was born in the possession of knowledge; I am one who is fond of antiquity, and earnest in seeking it there.

So even Confucius wasn't born wise. He worked at it.

He loved learning and kept seeking. Now here's where the Zen master Hui-neng adds a striking idea. The wisdom of enlightenment is inherent in every one of us.

Inherent. So it's already there, like Mencius's seeds.

Very similar. And Hui-neng has a lovely image for how fast it can appear. The light of a lamp can break up darkness which has been there for a thousand years.

That's hopeful. It doesn't matter how long you've been confused. One moment of clarity changes the room.

That's how many Buddhists read it. And the Buddha also insisted people test teachings for themselves. In the Kalama Sutta he says, Do not go by repeated hearing, nor by tradition, nor by rumor, nor by scripture, nor by logic alone, nor by the authority of a teacher.

That's surprising from a religious founder. Don't just take my word for it.

He continues that when you know for yourselves that something is good and leads to welfare and happiness, then you should take it up and live by it.

So wisdom has to be lived and tested.

Right. And the second way to uncover wisdom is accepting correction. Proverbs chapter nineteen says, Listen to advice and accept discipline, and at the end you will be counted among the wise.

That's the hard one. Nobody likes being corrected.

Which is exactly why it works. Correction shows you what you couldn't see about yourself.

And where does water come in?

Chapter eight of the Tao Te Ching. The highest excellence is like water. The excellence of water appears in its benefiting all things, and in its occupying, without striving, the low place which all men dislike.

The low place. So wisdom is humble.

Water doesn't argue. It goes low, it nourishes everything, and it finds its way around obstacles. And remember from the five virtues chapter, wisdom is linked to the element of water, and to the precept of no intoxicants.

Keeping the water clear.

Exactly. Clear water reflects. A clear mind sees itself.

How would I practice this today?

Here's one way. The next time someone corrects you, even on something small, pause before you defend yourself. Say thank you, and ask yourself honestly whether they might be right. Treat it as a lamp coming on.

That's going to be uncomfortable.

Usually it is. That's part of how you know it's working.

And the question to reflect on?

From the chapter. When did accepting correction make you wiser?

I can think of a teacher who told me something I didn't want to hear. She was right.

Thanks for listening to Five Wisdom Traditions.

item.title: Faith & Sincerity
item.description: Belief grounded in truth: Mencius and the Doctrine of the Mean on sincerity, the mustard seed, the Diamond Sutra's pure faith, and the line between faith and superstition.
item.content:encoded:
Belief grounded in truth: Mencius and the Doctrine of the Mean on sincerity, the mustard seed, the Diamond Sutra's pure faith, and the line between faith and superstition.

This is Five Wisdom Traditions. Today we come to the fifth constant virtue, faith, which the Primer also calls sincerity.

Faith and sincerity. Those seem like two different things.

The Primer ties them together in three short sentences. Faith originates from sincerity. The source of faith is truth. Faith is ascertained from wisdom.

So faith comes after wisdom, in a way. It sees where it's going.

That's the point. The series warns against two extremes. Here's how it puts it. Those who know about truth but do not believe in it are known as fools, and those who simply believe without the basis of truth are superstitious.

That's blunt. So you can fail by not believing what you know is true, or by believing what isn't.

Exactly. Real faith sits between them. It's belief grounded in truth.

Let's start with sincerity, then. What do the sages say?

Mencius says, Sincerity is the way of Heaven. To think how to be sincere is the way of man.

So Heaven is just naturally sincere, and we have to work at it.

Nicely summarized. And he goes on. Never has there been one possessed of complete sincerity who did not move others.

That rings true. You can tell when someone means it. It reaches you.

The Doctrine of the Mean, another of the Confucian Four Books, describes how to get there. He who attains to sincerity is he who chooses what is good, and firmly holds it fast.

Choose the good, then hold on. That's two steps. Most of us manage the first one.

Holding fast is where faith comes in. Remember, faith is linked to the element of earth, and to the precept of no lying.

Right. The ground. Steady. And you can't be sincere if you're lying.

Now, Jesus speaks about the power of faith in Matthew chapter seventeen. If you have faith as small as a mustard seed, you can say to this mountain, Move from here to there, and it will move.

A mustard seed is tiny.

That's the surprise. Jesus says even a little genuine faith can move a mountain. Christians often apply this to mountains of fear, illness or hopelessness.

And the Hebrew Bible has something on trust too, right?

Proverbs chapter three. Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding. In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths.

Lean not on your own understanding. Doesn't that clash with the idea that faith comes from wisdom?

Good question. One way to read it is that true wisdom includes knowing the limits of your own cleverness. Trust starts where your own understanding runs out.

That's a helpful way to hold both.

In Buddhism, the Diamond Sutra speaks of people who, hearing the teaching, will have an immediate uprising of pure faith. Pure faith there is a clear, settled confidence that comes from hearing the truth.

And Islam?

The Quran opens its second chapter, Surah Al-Baqarah, with this. This is the Book about which there is no doubt, a guidance for those conscious of God.

No doubt. That's confident language.

For Muslims it's the starting point. The book claims to be truth, and faith is the response to that truth. Which fits the Primer's sentence, the source of faith is truth.

So across the board, faith is a response to something real, and sincerity is what makes it genuine.

That's the thread. And you can see it in people. Their sincerity is what makes their faith believable to others.

So how do I practice this?

Here's a practice for today. Pick one promise you've made, to someone else or to yourself, and keep it fully. Be sincere in the small thing. Then notice how it feels to be someone whose word holds, like solid ground.

And the reflection question?

From the chapter. Whose sincerity has moved you?

My grandfather. He never said much, but when he said something, he meant it.

Thanks for listening to Five Wisdom Traditions.

item.title: Peacemaking & Forgiveness
item.description: Healing what divides us: the peacemakers of the Beatitudes, the Prophet Muhammad on making peace between enemies, the Buddha as healer of divisions, and Lao Tzu on answering anger with virtue.
item.content:encoded:
Healing what divides us: the peacemakers of the Beatitudes, the Prophet Muhammad on making peace between enemies, the Buddha as healer of divisions, and Lao Tzu on answering anger with virtue.

This is Five Wisdom Traditions. Today's chapter is about peacemaking and forgiveness, healing what divides us.

That feels especially relevant right now.

It always does. The Primer says the sages heal divisions. They reconcile before they worship, answer anger with virtue, and turn no one away.

Reconcile before they worship. Where does that come from?

From Jesus, in the Sermon on the Mount. Matthew chapter five. If you're bringing a gift to the altar and remember someone has something against you, he says, First go and be reconciled to your brother; then come and offer your gift.

So the relationship comes before the ritual.

Exactly. Earlier in the same sermon he says, Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God.

Peacemakers. That's an active word. It takes work.

And the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said something remarkable along the same lines. Shall I tell you what acts are better than fasting, charity, and prayers? Making peace between enemies.

Better than prayer? That's a strong ranking.

It shows how highly Islam values reconciliation. The Quran adds, And whoever is patient and forgives, indeed, that is of the matters requiring determination.

Requiring determination. So forgiveness takes strength.

That's the sense of it. And the Buddha is described in the Majjhima Nikaya this way. He heals divisions and cements friendships. His words are ever the words of a peacemaker.

I like the word cements. Friendships that hold.

The Dhammapada gives the Buddhist principle behind it. For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love. This is an old rule.

An old rule. Like it's always been true, we just keep forgetting.

And turning no one away has a Quranic root too. Surah Al-Hujurat says, O mankind! We created you from a male and a female, and made you into nations and tribes so that you may know one another.

So our differences are there to be explored. That's a peacemaker's starting point.

And Lao Tzu puts it in four words, in chapter sixty-three of the Tao Te Ching. Respond to anger with virtue.

Easy to say. Very hard in the moment.

Very hard. Lao Tzu has another line in chapter seventy-nine that helps. The sage honors his part of the settlement, but does not exact his due from others.

So you keep your side of the deal, even if they don't keep theirs.

Right. You stop keeping score. And that's close to how the series describes forgiveness. It says forgiveness does not have any purpose. If you can put yourself in another's shoes, this is a type of forgiveness.

No purpose. Meaning you're not forgiving to get something back.

That's how I read it. You forgive because you understand. When you see why someone acted the way they did, the anger loosens on its own.

And Jesus links forgiving to being forgiven, doesn't he?

In Luke chapter six. Forgive, and you will be forgiven. And it's in the Lord's Prayer, which Christians recite every day. And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.

That's sobering. You're asking to be forgiven the same way you forgive.

Many people find that a powerful daily reminder.

So what makes forgiveness so hard?

Often it feels like letting the other person off the hook, or like admitting the hurt didn't matter. The traditions say something different. The hurt mattered. Forgiveness frees you from carrying it.

And it's possible because, well, we all need it ourselves.

That's one of the deepest reasons, yes.

What's the practice for today?

Think of one person you're slightly at odds with. It doesn't have to be the biggest conflict in your life. Spend two minutes imagining the situation from their side. What were they afraid of? What did they need? Then, if you can, take one small step toward them. A message, a kind word, a coffee.

Small steps first.

And the reflection question is from the chapter. What makes forgiveness hard, and what makes it possible?

I think I'll be answering that one for a while.

Thanks for listening to Five Wisdom Traditions.

item.title: Introspection, Repentance & Vows
item.description: The cycle of self-correction: daily self-examination with Zengzi and Confucius, repentance as turning back in Paul, the Quran and the Avatamsaka Sutra, and vows that are truly kept.
item.content:encoded:
The cycle of self-correction: daily self-examination with Zengzi and Confucius, repentance as turning back in Paul, the Quran and the Avatamsaka Sutra, and vows that are truly kept.

This is Five Wisdom Traditions. Today we explore a cycle the Primer calls self-correction: introspection, repentance, and vows.

Three heavy words. Let's start with introspection.

The Primer's advice is simple. Look at yourself, not at others. Trace each mistake back to the thought behind it, and to the old concept behind that thought.

So a mistake has roots.

Deep ones. The series has a wonderful line about this. You were already wrong at the train station before you departed.

Ha. So by the time you notice you're lost, the error happened long ago, when you chose the train.

Exactly. And it warns, this is an effort, not knowledge; it cannot be attained by lip service.

What does introspection look like in practice?

Confucius's student Zengzi gives a model. I daily examine myself on three points: whether, in transacting business for others, I may have been not faithful; whether, in intercourse with friends, I may have been not sincere; whether I may have not mastered and practiced the instructions of my teacher.

Three questions every evening. Was I faithful at work, sincere with friends, and did I practice what I learned?

That's still a great daily review. And Confucius adds, When we see men of worth, we should think of equaling them; when we see men of a contrary character, we should turn inwards and examine ourselves.

I like that second half. When someone annoys me, I should check whether I do the same thing.

That's the hard part. Now, once you see the mistake, the next step is repentance. The Primer says repentance means turning back.

Turning back. Like making a U-turn.

Yes. The Zen master Hui-neng divides it into two parts. The first, called chan, is repenting past wrongs. The second, called hui, is resolving about future conduct.

So it's looking back and looking forward.

Both. Paul writes in Second Corinthians, Godly sorrow brings repentance that leads to salvation and leaves no regret.

Leaves no regret. That's interesting. Repentance should leave you lighter.

The Quran says something similar. Whoever repents and does righteous deeds, indeed he turns to Allah with true repentance.

Again, the turning.

And in the Avatamsaka Sutra, the bodhisattva Samantabhadra gives a confession many Buddhists recite. For all the evil deeds I have done in the past, I now know shame and repent them all.

That's very direct.

The practice, according to the Primer, is this. Every thought needs to be more positive and correct than the previous one.

That's ambitious. Every thought.

It's a direction. And that brings us to the third step, the vow. The Primer calls a vow an oath to keep one's mind under control, and the volition to fulfill it. It says a vow is not what is written on a piece of paper for you to simply pay lip service to.

So it's like a New Year's resolution, only serious.

Much more serious. Ecclesiastes chapter five warns, It is better not to make a vow than to make one and not fulfill it.

Better not to promise at all. Ouch.

Lao Tzu agrees. In chapter sixty-three he says, Easy promises make for little trust. And then, Because the sage always confronts difficulties, he never experiences them.

So the sage faces the hard thing early, while it's still small.

That's how the cycle connects. Look honestly. Turn back. Commit. Then look again.

Why do we keep repeating mistakes, though, even after we feel sorry?

The Primer's answer is in the roots. If you only regret the action and never trace it back to the thought and the concept behind it, the root grows back.

Here's my practice question then. What should I try today?

Tonight, before bed, try Zengzi's three questions. Then pick one mistake from the day and trace it back. What thought came before it, and what idea about yourself or others was behind that thought?

And the reflection question?

From the chapter. What vow would change your life if you truly kept it?

I'll make sure it's not an easy promise.

Thanks for listening to Five Wisdom Traditions.

item.title: Cause & Effect, Transforming Destiny
item.description: You reap what you sow: Paul, Jesus, the Quran, Hui-neng and Lao Tzu on cause and effect, and how thoughts become habits, character and destiny.
item.content:encoded:
You reap what you sow: Paul, Jesus, the Quran, Hui-neng and Lao Tzu on cause and effect, and how thoughts become habits, character and destiny.

This is Five Wisdom Traditions. Today we talk about cause and effect, and how the Primer says we can transform our destiny.

Destiny. Is that something these traditions believe in?

The Primer opens with a string of familiar sayings. Reap what you sow. What goes around comes around. Every action has an equal and opposite reaction. Karma.

Every culture has its version.

That's the point. Every tradition teaches some form of cause and effect. And so, the Primer says, destiny is not fixed. It is accumulated character, and it can be changed from within.

Okay, that's more hopeful than I expected. Let's hear the sources.

Paul writes to the Galatians, Whatever a man sows, that shall he also reap.

Straight farming logic. Plant wheat, get wheat.

And Jesus, when one of his followers draws a sword in the garden, says, All who draw the sword will die by the sword.

Violence comes back around.

The Quran puts it in personal terms. Whoever does a good deed, it is for himself; and whoever does evil, it is against himself.

So the first person affected by what I do is me.

In a sense, yes. And here's a verse that speaks directly to transforming destiny. Surely God changes not the condition of a people until they change what is in themselves.

That's powerful. The change starts inside.

The Buddha says the same thing in the opening lines of the Dhammapada. All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts.

And the result follows?

He says if a man speaks or acts with an evil thought, pain follows him, as the wheel follows the foot of the ox that draws the carriage. And if he acts with a pure thought, happiness follows him, like a shadow that never leaves him.

The wheel and the shadow. Those are vivid.

The series lays out the chain very clearly. Action after action will form a habit; habit after habit will form a concept; concept after concept will form a character; character after character will form a destiny.

So destiny is just the far end of a long chain that starts with tiny actions.

Exactly. Which means you can intervene at the start. The Primer says, transform the mind when the thought arises, while things are still small.

Lao Tzu must have something on that.

Chapter sixty-three of the Tao Te Ching. Take on difficulties while they are still easy. Do great things while they are still small. And chapter sixty-four. The journey of a thousand li commenced with a single step.

A li being a Chinese measure of distance.

Right. And Hui-neng locates all of it in the heart. All the fields of merit are within one's own heart.

So the field I'm planting is me.

Nicely said. Lao Tzu adds one more twist, in chapter fifty-eight. Calamity is what blessing depends upon; in blessing calamity lies hidden.

Meaning good and bad luck are tangled together?

Meaning we often can't tell in the moment. A setback can plant the seed of something good, and success can carry hidden risk. So you focus less on the outcome and more on the seeds.

This is reassuring, but also a bit demanding. I'm responsible for my thoughts.

The traditions would say that's the good news. If your thoughts got you here, your thoughts can take you somewhere else.

What's a practice for today?

Pick one habit you'd like to change. Today, just watch for the thought that comes right before it. The impulse to check your phone, to snap at someone, to put something off. When you catch the thought, pause for one breath. That's transforming the mind when the thought arises.

And the reflection question?

It's from the chapter. Based on your current thoughts, habits and character, what do you believe your destiny is? And if you don't like the answer, what mindset would you need to change to change it?

That's a sobering exercise. In a good way.

Thanks for listening to Five Wisdom Traditions.

item.title: The Path of Cultivation
item.description: Faith, repentance and vows, practice, accomplishment: the four steps of spiritual growth, the Doctrine of the Mean on the Path, and the lotus that blooms in the mud.
item.content:encoded:
Faith, repentance and vows, practice, accomplishment: the four steps of spiritual growth, the Doctrine of the Mean on the Path, and the lotus that blooms in the mud.

This is Five Wisdom Traditions. Today we follow what the Primer calls the path of cultivation, a map of spiritual growth in four steps.

Cultivation. Like a garden.

Very much like a garden. The four steps are faith, repentance and vows, practice, and accomplishment.

Let's go through them.

The first step, faith, is described as sharing one mind, one view and one practice with the divine.

So faith means lining yourself up with something greater.

That's a good way to say it. The second step, repentance and vows, is described as a counteracting force to karma. The instruction is, treat everything as a cause.

Treat everything as a cause. So every moment is a seed for what comes next.

Right. The third step is practice. Every thought, word and action more positive and correct than the previous one.

We heard that one in the repentance chapter.

We did. It keeps coming back because it's the heart of the work. And the fourth step is accomplishment, which the Primer describes as testifying with your own experience.

So in the end, you show it with your life.

Exactly. Now, the Primer roots this path in a line from the Doctrine of the Mean. What Heaven has conferred is called the nature; an accordance with this nature is called the Path.

So the path is right here. Living by your own nature.

Your Heaven-given nature, yes. The same text says, The superior man can find himself in no situation in which he is not himself.

I love that. Wherever you are, you're still you.

Whether rich or poor, honored or overlooked. Jesus says something similar about priorities in Matthew chapter six. Consider the lilies. And then, But seek first the kingdom of God.

The lilies don't worry about clothes.

And yet they're beautifully dressed. Jesus also stresses the practice step. In Matthew chapter seven he says, Everyone who hears these words of mine and puts them into practice is like a wise man who built his house on the rock.

So hearing is only the start. Then you build.

Now the emblem of this whole chapter is the lotus. It grows in mud yet blossoms pure. The series asks, how does one remain a lotus in the midst of the muddy world?

That's the question, isn't it? Life is muddy.

And the Vimalakirti Sutra makes a bold claim. It is only within the mud of the afflictions that sentient beings give rise to the dharmas of a buddha.

So the mud is necessary. You can't grow the flower without it.

That's how many Buddhists read it. Your struggles are the soil. The Bhagavad Gita, from the Hindu tradition, uses the same image. As the lotus leaf is untouched by water.

The water rolls right off.

Right. You live fully in the world without being soaked through by it.

Where does Lao Tzu fit?

Chapter forty-eight of the Tao Te Ching describes cultivation as subtraction. He who devotes himself to learning seeks from day to day to increase his knowledge; he who devotes himself to the Tao seeks from day to day to diminish his doing.

So growing spiritually is partly letting things go.

Yes. And the Primer mentions one more support, rites and seasons. The new year, Lent and Ramadan return us to our nature.

That's why traditions repeat them every year. A chance to start again.

Exactly. A ritual is a reset button that the whole community presses together.

So what's the practice for today?

Choose one ordinary moment you repeat every day. Making coffee, brushing your teeth, locking the door. Turn it into a small ritual. Take one breath and set an intention for the next hour. Let the repetition bring you back to yourself.

And the reflection question?

From the chapter. What is the mud in your life right now, and what could bloom from it?

I think I'm standing knee-deep in the answer.

Thanks for listening to Five Wisdom Traditions.

item.title: The Six Paramitas
item.description: Six perfections for crossing to the other shore: donation, precepts, endurance, diligence, meditation and wisdom, with parallels from Jesus, the Quran, Proverbs and Lao Tzu.
item.content:encoded:
Six perfections for crossing to the other shore: donation, precepts, endurance, diligence, meditation and wisdom, with parallels from Jesus, the Quran, Proverbs and Lao Tzu.

This is Five Wisdom Traditions. Today we look at the six paramitas, Buddhism's six perfections for crossing to the other shore.

The other shore. That's a Buddhist image for awakening?

Yes. Paramita means perfection, and it's often explained as going beyond, crossing the river of suffering. The six give a practical training, and the series finds a parallel to each one in the other traditions.

Six is a lot. Let's go quickly.

The first is donation. The Primer says, to give without a stingy mind, whether wealth, teaching or fearlessness, and without clinging to the merit of the gift.

Giving fearlessness. I like that. Calming someone down is a gift.

Jesus teaches the same humility about giving. When you give to the needy, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing.

Don't keep score, even with yourself.

And the Quran agrees. If you disclose your charitable expenditures, they are good; but if you conceal them and give them to the poor, it is better for you. The Buddha adds, in the Dhammapada, Give, even if you only have a little.

So nobody's excused.

The second paramita is the precepts. The Primer says, by controlling oneself, one is freed from outside temptation. And it notes that the five precepts parallel the Ten Commandments.

No killing, no stealing, no lying. They do line up.

The third is endurance, or patience. The series quotes a saying, One endurance can bring thousands of auspiciousness, and to yield one step can increase hundreds of blessings.

Yield one step. That's hard when I'm sure I'm right.

Proverbs chapter fifteen backs it up. He who is slow to anger quiets contention. And the Dhammapada says, If one man conquer in battle a thousand times thousand men, and if another conquer himself, he is the greatest of conquerors.

The fourth?

Diligence, which the Primer calls steady, joyful effort. Lao Tzu's chapter seven hints at its secret. Why do Heaven and Earth last forever? Because they do not live for themselves.

Effort lasts longer when it serves something beyond you.

Exactly. The fifth is meditation. And the Primer is careful here. It says, Manifest calm and serene without falling into emptiness. And it explains two terms. Dhyana is freedom from attachment to outer things, and samadhi is inner peace. It is not just sitting still.

Good, because I'm terrible at sitting still.

Jesus points to the same inner place. The kingdom of God is within you. And Lao Tzu describes the letting go that meditation needs. Those who seek knowledge collect something every day. Those who seek the Way let go of something every day.

And the sixth?

Wisdom, or prajna. The Primer says, All wisdom comes from the essence of mind and not from an exterior source. And it adds that wisdom is manifested in how you handle situations.

So wisdom shows up in action.

Right. And Hui-neng says it can turn in a single moment. A foolish passing thought makes one an ordinary person, while an enlightened second thought makes one a Buddha.

An enlightened second thought. That's encouraging. The first thought might be foolish, but I get another try.

That's one of the most hopeful lines in the whole Primer. Every moment offers a second thought.

So six perfections. Giving, self-control, patience, effort, calm, and wisdom.

And they build on each other. Giving loosens your grip. Precepts steady you. Patience and effort carry you. Calm clears the mind. And wisdom appears in how you live.

What's the practice for today?

Pick the paramita you need most today. If it's patience, the next time you're irritated, yield one step and see what happens. If it's giving, do one kind thing quietly and tell no one.

And the reflection question?

From the chapter. What tries your patience, and why?

Traffic. And I suspect the why is more interesting than the what.

Thanks for listening to Five Wisdom Traditions.

item.title: The Five Human Relationships
item.description: Where virtue is actually lived: the duties on both sides of each relationship, three levels of filial piety, love in marriage, and what makes a true friend.
item.content:encoded:
Where virtue is actually lived: the duties on both sides of each relationship, three levels of filial piety, love in marriage, and what makes a true friend.

This is Five Wisdom Traditions. Today we look at the five human relationships, which the Primer calls the place where virtue is actually lived.

That makes sense. It's easy to be virtuous alone in a room.

Exactly. The Primer follows the Great Learning, one of the Confucian Four Books. Cultivating yourself regulates the family, a regulated family steadies the nation, and an orderly nation brings peace to the world.

So world peace starts with me. No pressure.

And each relationship carries a duty on both sides. The first is superior and subordinate. Think boss, teacher, coach. The one above owes benevolence and care. The one below owes loyalty and respect.

Both sides have a job.

Confucius says, A prince should employ his ministers according to the rules of propriety; ministers should serve their prince with faithfulness. And Mencius adds a vivid picture. When the prince regards his ministers as his hands and feet, his ministers regard their prince as their belly and heart.

So if a boss treats people as part of the body, they'll protect the boss like their own heart.

That's it. The second relationship is parents and children. Parents owe love and kindness, and children owe filial piety.

Respect for parents.

The Primer describes three levels of filial piety. Small is material support for the body. Medium is respect and obedience for the mind. And great is using your own virtue to help your parents' spiritual well-being.

That third one is beautiful. Becoming a better person is a gift to your parents.

The Quran expresses the tenderness of this relationship. And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy, and say: My Lord, have mercy upon them as they brought me up when I was small.

The wing of humility. Like a bird sheltering its young, only now reversed.

Exactly. The third relationship is husband and wife. The Primer says they have different responsibilities, working together, with mutual respect, forgiveness and trust. And it adds a memorable warning. If there is only reason and logic but no love and affection between husband and wife, then it is like a judge trying a criminal.

Oof. I think every couple has had that conversation.

The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said, The most perfect believer in faith is the one whose character is finest and who is kindest to his wife. And First Peter in the New Testament says, Most important of all, continue to show deep love for each other, for love covers a multitude of sins.

Love covers a multitude of sins. That's a good marriage motto.

The fourth relationship is between elder and younger siblings. The elder takes care of the younger, and the younger respects the elder.

And the fifth is friends.

Friendship rests on mutual trust. Friends are righteous, trustworthy, diligent. Proverbs chapter seventeen says, A friend loves at all times, and a brother is born for a time of adversity.

So you find out who your friends are in hard times.

And true friends are honest. Proverbs chapter twenty-seven says, Wounds from a friend can be trusted, but an enemy multiplies kisses. The Dhammapada agrees. Should you find a wise critic to point out your faults, follow him as you would a guide to hidden treasure.

A guide to hidden treasure. That's a generous way to think about criticism.

And Mencius says, Friendship with a man is friendship with his virtue, and does not admit of assumptions of superiority.

So friends meet as equals.

Right. Across all five, the same virtues show up. Benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom and faith, lived with real people.

What's a practice for today?

Choose one of the five relationships in your own life. Ask what your side of the duty is, and do one concrete thing to fulfill it. Call a parent to say thank you. Encourage someone you supervise. Tell a friend something honest and kind.

And the reflection question?

From the chapter. How can we become a better friend?

I think I'll start by being the wise critic and the steady one in hard times.

Thanks for listening to Five Wisdom Traditions.

item.title: Awakening
item.description: The questions that start the journey: the narrow gate, the Tao that cannot be named, Confucius's stages of a life, and how the common principles of the Primer ground any awakening.
item.content:encoded:
The questions that start the journey: the narrow gate, the Tao that cannot be named, Confucius's stages of a life, and how the common principles of the Primer ground any awakening.

This is Five Wisdom Traditions. Today we reach the final chapter of the Primer, on awakening, and the questions that start the journey.

The last chapter. How does the series end?

It ends where it began, with the oldest questions. Why are you born into this world, and for what purpose? Why do you age, get sick and die?

Those are the questions the young Buddha asked, aren't they?

They're the questions behind his search, yes. And the Primer says each tradition speaks of a truth beyond words.

Beyond words. That's hard to talk about on a podcast.

It is. But the sages tried. Jesus calls it the narrow gate. In Matthew chapter seven he says, Enter through the narrow gate.

Narrow because it's hard to find? Or because few choose it?

Christians have read it both ways. It's a path that asks something of you. Lao Tzu opens the Tao Te Ching with his version. The Tao that can be trodden is not the enduring and unchanging Tao. The name that can be named is not the enduring and unchanging name.

So the moment you put it in words, you've missed it.

Right. And Zen describes its teaching as transmitted outside the scriptures. Something passed from heart to heart.

That fits Hui-neng, who we've heard so much from.

It does. Buddhism points at this truth in the Heart Sutra, which many Buddhists chant daily. Form is emptiness, emptiness is form. Emptiness is not other than form; form is not other than emptiness.

I'll admit I don't fully understand that.

Few people claim to. One reading is that everything we cling to as solid and separate is more open and connected than it looks. Seeing that is part of awakening.

What about Islam?

The opening chapter of the Quran, Al-Fatiha, which Muslims recite in every prayer, contains a request for exactly this. Guide us on the straight path.

So even daily prayer is a request to wake up and stay on course.

That's a lovely way to put it. Now, the Primer adds that several of the sages looked ahead to an age when that truth would be awakened again. Confucius spoke of waiting for the rise of a sage a hundred ages after. And the Diamond Sutra speaks of an uprising of pure faith long after the Buddha.

So awakening belongs to every age.

The series would say it's for any of us. Confucius himself describes a lifetime of it in the Analects, book two. At fifteen, I had my mind bent on learning. At thirty, I stood firm. At forty, I had no doubts. At fifty, I knew the decrees of Heaven.

Keep going. What happens at the end?

At sixty, my ear was an obedient organ for the reception of truth. At seventy, I could follow what my heart desired, without transgressing what was right.

That last stage sounds like freedom. What you want and what's right become the same thing.

That's how many people read it. And notice it took him a lifetime. Awakening, in this picture, is a long walk.

So how does the Primer tie everything together?

Its closing thought is this. The common principles in this primer, the five virtues, honest self-examination, cause and effect, and love lived out in every relationship, are the ground on which any awakening stands.

So the virtues come first, and enlightenment grows from them.

Exactly. Kindness, fairness, respect, clear seeing, and honesty come first. They're the soil. And the Primer says the passages in the app are a place to practice them, one day at a time.

I find that comforting. Awakening sounds huge, but the steps are small.

Here's a practice for today. Read one passage from any tradition slowly, twice. Then choose one sentence from it to carry with you all day. Let it come back to you at odd moments, and notice what it wakes up.

And our final reflection question?

From the chapter. What would you need to let go of to begin?

Maybe the idea that I'll start tomorrow.

Thanks for listening to Five Wisdom Traditions.
